description: Grounds for Thought: October 2026 (Defence Colony)A Blue Tokai × unLecture SeriesGrounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. October runs across Delhi and Bangalore, moving from temple sculpture to constitutional pedagogy, from parenting in the AI age to the politics of a Bollywood item number.1st October: Dolan SamantaTemple sculpture is usually read as devotion — divine bodies carved to be worshipped. This session argues it does something more: these images are sites where gender, desire, and authority are negotiated, not just depicted. Taking two ninth-to-eleventh-century carvings of Śiva and Pārvatī from the Nīlakaṇṭha temple at Kālañjara as its central text, and reading them through Puranic myth, Foucault, and Judith Butler's account of gender as performance, Dolan Samanta, a history educator and JNU-trained researcher, asks why Śiva appears nude, enraged, and armed, his sexuality fused with dominance, while Pārvatī appears smaller, modest, at once desired and desiring. The question stone carved a thousand years ago still puts to us: who was permitted power, and who was only expected to receive it?8th October: Tania KapoorMost parents still treat marks as the surest route to a child's future — but school mostly rewards memorising, following instructions, and reproducing the right answer in the right way, exactly the kind of work AI is fastest at absorbing. Tania Kapoor, a Delhi-based child and adolescent psychologist trained at AIIMS, argues that what will actually distinguish children going forward — adaptability, emotional regulation, impulse control, comfort with ambiguity — is precisely what classrooms and busy households keep treating as something to address "later" Grounded in clinical practice, this session asks what parents should be paying attention to now, before later becomes too late.15th October: Dr. Jasleen RanaEvery purchase carries a story that has little to do with the product itself — emotion, aspiration, insecurity, identity. Dr. Jasleen Rana, who holds a PhD in Consumer Psychology and teaches Marketing at JIMS Kalkaji, moves past the question of what we buy to the more revealing one why. Through brand archetypes, hidden motivations, and everyday examples — choosing one coffee shop over another, paying more for a brand that does exactly what a cheaper one does — this interactive session decodes the psychological triggers behind consumer choice, and what those choices reveal about identity, belonging, and self-image.22nd October: Shubham YadavWhat if ordinary citizens believed they had something to teach the members of the Constituent Assembly? Shubham Yadav, a Senior Research Fellow at JNU's Zakir Husain Centre for Educational Studies, argues that India's Constitution wasn't shaped by elites alone — it emerged from a running exchange in which both "the people" and "the makers" wanted to instruct each other on what the new nation should be. Framed as a conversation rather than a lecture, the session traces that two-way pedagogy, and what it reveals about how theConstitution actually came to be built.

name: When AI Starts Inventing
description: When AI Starts Inventing: How AI Is Cracking Problems That Have Resisted Us for Decades, and How to Bring It from Big Tech's Labs to Your LaptopIn September 2026, OpenAI announced that a team of AI agents had produced a proof, machine-verified in Lean, for a problem about how fluids move that has stood open for ninety years and carries a million-dollar prize. Before that, an AI agent found a faster way to multiply matrices, the operation that sits underneath almost all modern computing, beating a record set in 1969. It is starting to feel routine: every few weeks, another problem that resisted people for decades quietly falls to an AI agent.How does this actually happen? That is what we will look at first, because the mechanism turns out to be stranger and simpler than most people expect.Then a harder question. Every time the agent is asked to produce something, someone pays, and the more capable the AI, the higher the bill. A single discovery run makes thousands of such calls, which is why almost all of this work happens inside a handful of enormously wealthy labs. In our lab we are trying to change that, and doing so means asking questions nobody bothers to ask when the budget is unlimited. Does every step really need the most expensive AI model, or would a cheaper one do just as well? Is every attempt the agent makes actually worth making? Our investigation of these discovery pipelines, across several notoriously hard problems, reveals that around 98% of the AI agent's calls contribute nothing to the eventual solution. And they still succeed. Which leaves a genuinely open question: is that waste the price of discovery, or simply a bill nobody has bothered to reduce?About the SpeakerProf. Sayan Ranu is the DS Chair Professor in AI at IIT Delhi, jointly appointed in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering and the Yardi School of AI. His research focuses on machine learning for structured data, particularly graphs, and increasingly on AI systems that can reason, plan and discover solutions on their own. His work spans automated algorithm discovery, AI agents, self-supervised learning and trustworthy AI. His research has been published at leading AI and machine learning conferences including NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR and KDD. He was also a recipient of the Teaching Excellence Award at IIT Delhi and currently serves as a Senior Area Chair for NeurIPS 2026 and Program Co-Chair for the Datasets & Benchmarks Track at KDD 2027.Book now & develop your own pint of view! 🍻

name: Rewriting Epics The Feminist Way
description: About the LectureThe Epics have held the Indian imagination since time immemorial, narrated, performed and rendered into cinema again and again. Looking at them afresh means asking the questions they've spent centuries deflecting: the role of women, the contribution of the dispossessed, and the quintessential human questions of survival and existence.A feminist retelling brings the women back to the centre. It strips away the proverbial sheen of the "just" war to focus on the human question underneath. Whether it's the fiery Draupadi, the "manipulative" Satyavati, the warrior queen Chitrangada, Janaki, or the duo of Kaikeyi and Manthara, the Epics allow us to deconstruct these women through a modern feminist lens.The session explores:How feminist retellings of the Mahabharata and Ramayana recentre their women charactersWhat writers like Tagore, Mahasweta Devi, Irawati Karve and Chitra Divakaruni reveal through their retellingsWhy the Epics' "timeless" characters remain contemporary and urgently relevantHow deconstructing canonical narratives changes what the stories are actually aboutAbout the SpeakerDr. Nandini C. Sen is a Professor of English at the University of Delhi — an author, editor, literary critic and storyteller. For nearly three decades, she has explored how literature shapes the way we understand history, identity, gender and the world around us, working across African Literature, Diaspora studies, mythology, postcolonial studies and feminist readings of the Indian epics. Her academic journey has taken her from Delhi to London as a Charles Wallace Scholar, to the Indian Institute of Advanced Study, Shimla as a Fellow, and to universities and literary forums across the world. She is the recipient of the Write India Award for creative writing, the Ambassador for Peace Prize for teaching in a slum cluster, and the Best Lecturer's Award from the Government of Delhi. description: About the LectureA raised eyebrow. A shift in posture. A half-second pause before an answer. Long before you finish a sentence, your body has usually already told the room the truth.This lecture explores body language as one of the most powerful forms of communication we have. name: Cultures Through Clay: Civilisation Held In A Bowl
description: About the LectureWe sometimes just think of pots as functional. But across three cultures — Bangladesh, Turkey and Japan — the same simple act of shaping wet clay reveals three completely different value systems: community and belonging, beauty and craftsmanship, imperfection and impermanence.This talk isn't really about pottery. It's about how to read the objects around us, and what your own everyday things might be quietly saying about you.Drawing on folklorist Henry Glassie's The Potter's Art, the session zooms into three pottery traditions: in Bangladesh, pottery woven into caste, community and everyday ritual life; in Turkey, pottery as a vessel for aesthetic pride and decorative mastery; and in Japan's Hagi tradition, tied to the tea ceremony, where the values invert entirely — imperfection, asymmetry and impermanence, the wabi-sabi aesthetic, are not flaws to correct but the entire point.The session explores:How the same craft, shaping wet clay, produces radically different worlds of meaning across culturesWhat pottery in Bangladesh, Turkey and Japan reveals about caste, beauty and impermanenceWhy folk art is never really anonymous, static or purely functionalWhat your own everyday objects might be quietly saying about what you valueAbout the Speaker Simran Sushila is a folklorist and a professor, currently pursuing her PhD in Folklore at Indiana University Bloomington, USA. description: Grounds for Thought: October 2026 (Janpath)A Blue Tokai × unLecture SeriesGrounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. October runs across Delhi and Bangalore, moving from temple sculpture to constitutional pedagogy, from parenting in the AI age to the politics of a Bollywood item number.6th October: Harshit BishtYour phone finishes your sentences, your inbox drafts your replies, a chatbot will happily name your business for you — and it's doing the same for millions of other people at once. Harshit Bisht, a PhD scholar in artificial intelligence at IIT Delhi researching multimodal foundation models for scientific discovery, asks what happens when systems trained on existing culture start setting the default for what counts as a "good" or "natural" answer, across countries, languages, and ways of seeing the world. Built around everyday experience rather than technical background, the session isn't trying to settle whether AI is good or bad — only what happens to the differences between us as these tools get better at helping each of us individually.13th October: Prerna VatsWords like "comprehensive," "flexible," and "excellence" fill education policy documents, but what do they mean once they reach an actual classroom — and who decides? Prerna Vats, a PhD scholar in Women and Gender Studies at Ambedkar University and a teacher trainer and sexuality educator, reads the National Education Policy 2020 alongside Krishna Kumar's 1992 text What Is Worth Teaching to trace the gap between education's imagined goals and its measurable outcomes. The session puts the figure of the teacher — and participants' own educational journeys — at the centre, asking who gets left out in the pursuit of "quality" education.27th October: Abhishek PanchalClimate communication has leaned so heavily on doomsday narratives that it often produces disengagement instead of action, while pseudo-sustainable habits let people feel involved without shifting the underlying politics. Abhishek Panchal, a research scientist at Ashoka University and former ISRO scientist-engineer, introduces Pralay, a cooperative strategy board game where players navigate competing climate priorities at the individual, state, and global level. Built on storytelling and discussion rather than lecture, the session asks whether an evening around a game table can do what doomsday statistics haven't — and examines whether it actually shifts attitudes, not just conversation.

name: Can We Make Delhi a Human City?
description: Welcome to Human City Conversations where we have intimate conversations about how cities are built, how they are lived, and who gets to shape them.Conversation 1: HOW DO WE MAKE DELHI A HUMAN CITY?Delhi is a city of contradictions. It has some of India's best public institutions, an expanding metro network, enormous infrastructure projects and a new Master Plan for Delhi 2047 that sets out a vision for how the city should grow and change over the next two decades. And yet, the experience of living in Delhi can be very different.Millions of people spend hours commuting across the city. Walking can feel like an afterthought. Public spaces are often unevenly distributed and poorly connected. For many women, moving through the city comes with a calculation of safety that men may never have to make. And then there is the air. Every winter, Delhi's air pollution becomes a public health crisis forcing a city of millions to think about something as fundamental as whether it is safe to breathe outside.So how can a city with so much planning, infrastructure and investment still struggle with some of the most basic conditions of everyday urban life? Perhaps the problem is not simply how much we build, perhaps we need to ask a more fundamental question:What kind of city are we actually trying to build? And more importantly, who is that city being built for?For the first Human City Conversation, urbanist Jagan Shah joins Ruchita Bansal for an open conversation about Delhi, its future and the gap between the city we plan on paper and the city people actually experience. We'll explore what makes a city genuinely liveable from mobility and housing to public space, safety, air pollution and neighbourhoods and look at what Delhi's new Master Plan for 2047 could mean on the ground.What to ExpectA curated, open conversation between urbanist Jagan Shah and Ruchita BansalA look at Delhi's urban future and what the new Master Plan for Delhi 2047 could mean on the groundA discussion about the gap between the city we plan and the city people actually experienceA closer look at how cities are shaped by policies, infrastructure and development decisionsPerspectives on what makes a city genuinely liveable, accessible and inclusiveA 30 minute Q&A SessionInformal discussion and one on one conversation after the conversationEvent Details📅 Sunday, 11 October 2026🕔 5:00 PM onwards📍 Kunzum Books, GK II, Delhi☕ Your ticket includes one coffee/tea .About the SpeakerJagan Shah is an urbanist, architect and former Director of the National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA), with decades of experience working at the intersection of urban planning, policy, governance and development. He has been closely involved in shaping India's urban policy and planning landscape, including work connected to Delhi's Master Plan, the Smart Cities Mission and other national urban development programmes. His work has involved developing and implementing policies and frameworks that influence how Indian cities grow, transform and respond to the challenges of rapid urbanisation.Over the years, Jagan has worked across urban planning, housing, infrastructure, heritage, governance and institutional development, working with governments and institutions at different levels.His experience spans both the making of plans and policies and the realities of implementing them, making him particularly well placed to examine the gap between the city we envision on paper and the city that people actually experience.About the ModeratorRuchita Bansal is an architect and urban planner with 15 years of experience working on cities, urban development and planning policy. Her work has ranged from developing planning frameworks and regulations to working directly on large-scale urban transformation projects. She was part of the team behind Ayodhya Vision 2047, working on one of India's most complex and rapidly transforming urban environments and seeing first-hand the challenges of translating ambitious plans and visions into reality on the ground.Today, Ruchita is the Creator and Host of The Human City Podcast and the founder of SheCity India, using conversations, research and storytelling to make urban planning more accessible and bring the discussion about cities beyond the professional planning community. Through The Human City, she explores a simple but often overlooked question: what does all this planning mean for the people who actually live in our cities?Note: Attendance implies consent to being filmed for event documentation. If you do not wish to be filmed, please reach out to your curator for the evening, Ruchita. Come curious. Come questioning. Come ready to talk about the city we call home.

description: Mehfil-e-Yashraj ~ An unforgettable evening of ghazalYashraj is a remarkably talented 12-year-old ghazal and Sufi singer who has already created a growing audience through social media platforms such as Facebook and Instagram. Despite his young age, he has participated in and won several state-level music competitions and is also a Sangam Kala Group winner.His soulful and soothing voice has earned him appreciation and blessings from renowned personalities of the ghazal and music fraternity, including Ustaad Ghulam Ali Khan Sahib and Murshid Ali. His musical journey is deeply rooted in the guidance of his guru, Sh. Sudhanshu Ehsaas, who has been nurturing and training him since Yashraj was just six years old.The talent that Yashraj displays today is the result of years of dedicated riyaaz, discipline, learning and hard work—both by the young artist and his guru. His understanding of music, command over ghazal and Sufi compositions, and his naturally peaceful and expressive voice make him a truly promising young performer. Depot 48 provide talented singers and performers with a platform where they can build their artistic profile, gain confidence and, most importantly, experience the energy and dynamics of a live audience.For Yashraj, this opportunity is especially meaningful. At just 12, he already possesses the musical ability of a seasoned young artist, while live audience engagement is naturally an area where he will continue to grow with experience. With more stage exposure, interactions with diverse audiences and continued riyaaz, he has immense potential to develop into a confident and compelling live performer.
